overview: Nok names an archaeological tradition of central Nigeria, recognized through pottery, terracotta sculpture and, during part of its history, iron production. Excavations do not establish a single kingdom.

items.text: Terracotta production flourished during the first millennium BCE. Broken figures sometimes occur in deposits interpreted as ritual, although their original meanings remain uncertain.
Charred pearl millet grains document farming. Grinding equipment and pottery provide further evidence of food preparation.
Furnaces show iron smelting during the Middle Nok period. Their radiocarbon dates cannot resolve a precise invention year.
Chemical residues in pottery identify processing of bee products, probably including honey. The study does not establish domesticated beekeeping.
Researchers interpret many settlements as small farming communities. Elaborate sculpture alone does not demonstrate centralized government or a rigid social hierarchy.

sources.title: Peter Breunig and Nicole Rupp, An Outline of Recent Studies on the Nigerian Nok Culture (2016)
Julie Dunne et al., Honey-collecting in prehistoric West Africa from 3500 years ago (2021)
